mcqs.question: Model A has errors [2,2,2,2] (MAE = 2). Model B has errors [1,1,1,5] (MAE = 2). Same MAE — which metric will rank them differently, and how?
options: RMSE — it will show Model B as worse because of the one large error
MAE — it will show Model B as worse once you recompute it carefully
R² — it will show Model A as worse because it explains less variance
Precision@k — not applicable to regression, so it will show them as equal
mcqs.explanation: RMSE squares errors, so Model B's single 5 dominates the average and pushes RMSE well above Model A's — even though both have identical MAE. MAE is linear and genuinely ties them. R² measures variance explained, not a direct per-point comparison like this. Precision@k is a ranking metric, unrelated to numeric regression error.

mcqs.question: You evaluate a regression model on held-out test data and R² comes out negative. What does that mean?
options: The predicted and actual values are negatively correlated
R² is a probability and can't go below 0, so this signals a bug in the code
The model's predictions are worse than simply predicting the mean of the target every time
The model is overfitting the training data
mcqs.explanation: Negative R² means SS_res exceeds SS_tot — the model's errors are larger than just guessing the target's mean for every prediction. It's not a probability and isn't inherently a bug. Overfitting can contribute, but that's not what negative R² directly measures — it's about the test-set fit being worse than a trivial baseline.

mcqs.question: A search page returns 10 results, 4 of which are relevant, out of 20 relevant products that exist in the catalog. What is Recall@10?
mcqs.explanation: Recall@k divides relevant items retrieved by the total relevant items that exist: 4 / 20 = 0.2. 4/10 is actually Precision@10, a common mix-up between the two metrics.

mcqs.question: Two ranked lists contain the exact same 3 relevant items within their top 5, just in a different order. Will they get the same NDCG?
options: No — NDCG discounts by rank position, so ordering matters even with identical item sets
Yes — NDCG only checks set membership, the same way Precision@k does
Yes — NDCG is undefined whenever two lists share the same items
No — but only because the item sets must actually differ for NDCG to differ
mcqs.explanation: NDCG's discount term divides each item's relevance by log2(position+1), so the same relevant items score differently depending on how high they rank. Precision@k, unlike NDCG, would treat both lists as identical since it only checks set membership.

mcqs.question: Team A reports RMSE = 50 forecasting daily website visits (average ~500/day). Team B reports RMSE = 50,000 forecasting annual revenue (average ~$500,000,000). Which model is more accurate relative to its target?
options: Team A, since 50 is a much smaller raw number than 50,000
Team B — its RMSE is only about 0.01% of its average target value, versus Team A's 10%
They're equally accurate since RMSE isn't comparable across different problems at all
It can't be determined without also knowing each model's R²
mcqs.explanation: Normalizing RMSE by the target's mean shows Team B's error is roughly 0.01% of target versus Team A's 10% — Team B is actually far more accurate despite the much bigger raw RMSE. That's exactly why comparing raw RMSE across different scales is misleading; normalizing (or using R²) fixes it rather than making comparison impossible.
